topics.title: swaplevel exchanges two levels
topics.body: A MultiIndex keeps the level names, and `swaplevel` exchanges their order so the report sorts by the other dimension without rebuilding the groupby.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune"], "year": [2026], "v": [1]})
s = df.groupby(["city", "year"])["v"].sum()
print(s.swaplevel().index.names)

topics.title: pd.NA is the missing scalar
topics.body: `pd.NA` is the missing value of the nullable dtypes, distinct from `np.nan`. `isna()` recognises both, which is why a test should use it rather than an equality check.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, pd.NA], dtype="Int64")
print(s.isna().tolist())
print(s.fillna(0).tolist())

topics.title: pipe can pass arguments
topics.body: `pipe` forwards extra arguments to the function, so one reusable step can be parameterised without a lambda.

topics.title: query can read a local variable
topics.body: An `@name` inside a query refers to a Python variable, which lets a threshold come from config while the condition stays a readable string.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

limit = 2
df = pd.DataFrame({"v": [1, 2, 3]})
print(df.query("v > @limit")["v"].tolist())

interview.q: When is a MultiIndex worth the verbosity?
interview.answer: When a result is genuinely two-dimensional and the second dimension is a category such as year, and when cross-sections with `xs` replace repeated filtering. For a single flat report, `reset_index` is easier to read.

interview.q: What does Copy-on-Write change for a learner?
interview.answer: A slice behaves like a copy for writes: modifying a derived frame no longer changes the parent silently, and chained assignment either fails or does nothing. The fix is one `.loc` call on the frame you intend to change.

topics.title: skew tells you which way the tail runs
topics.body: `skew()` is positive when the long tail is on the right and negative when it is on the left. It quantifies what a mean far above the median already hinted at.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

print(round(float(pd.Series([1, 1, 1, 100]).skew()), 2))
print(round(float(pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4]).skew()), 2))

topics.title: corr takes a method
topics.body: Pearson measures linear agreement; Spearman ranks the values first, so it survives a curved but monotone relationship and is the safer default on ordinal data.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": [1, 4, 9, 16]})
print(round(df["a"].corr(df["b"]), 2), round(df["a"].corr(df["b"], method="spearman"), 2))

topics.title: qcut makes equal-count buckets
topics.body: `cut` splits by value ranges; `qcut` splits into groups of roughly equal size. Deciles of spend need qcut, because a fixed range would put almost everyone in one bucket.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
print(pd.qcut(s, 3).value_counts().sort_index().tolist())

topics.title: describe(include='all') covers text
topics.body: The default summary skips text. `include="all"` adds count, unique and top for the object columns, which is the difference between a numeric profile and a full one.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"], "v": [1, 2]})
print(df.describe(include="all").shape[0])

interview.q: How do you turn an EDA observation into a finding?
interview.answer: Name the segment, give the metric with its denominator, and state what would falsify it. "Pune learners pass at 62% of 812 attempts" is a finding; "Pune looks better" is an impression.

interview.q: What is Simpson's paradox in a Pandas table?
interview.answer: An overall trend that reverses inside every segment, because the segments differ in size and baseline. Group by the segment and compare the relationship within groups before reporting the pooled number.

topics.title: astype narrows a numeric column
topics.body: The smallest integer dtype that fits the range can cut memory by a factor of four or more. Check the min and max first, because an overflowing cast is silent.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 127], dtype="int64")
print(s.astype("int8").nbytes)
print(s.astype("int8").max())

topics.title: category codes are integers
topics.body: `cat.codes` exposes the integer behind each category, which is a compact feature column while the readable labels stay available.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["b", "a", "b"], dtype="category")
print(s.cat.codes.tolist())
print(s.cat.categories.tolist())

topics.title: eval computes against columns by name
topics.body: `eval` parses one expression and evaluates it against the frame, which avoids building every intermediate column of a long formula.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
print(df.eval("(a + b) * 2").tolist())

topics.title: A chunk loop keeps one frame alive
topics.body: Aggregating inside the loop means only the current chunk exists; appending each chunk to a list and concatenating at the end rebuilds the full table in memory.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

total = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(StringIO("v\n1\n2\n3"), chunksize=2):
    total += int(chunk["v"].sum())
print(total)

interview.q: What is the first performance change you try on a slow Pandas pipeline?
interview.answer: Find the row-wise step: `iterrows` or `apply(axis=1)` is usually where the time goes. Rewrite it as column arithmetic or a groupby transform, then measure again rather than assuming.

interview.q: Why is a naive `int8` downcast risky?
interview.answer: The cast does not raise on overflow; it wraps to a negative number. Check min and max against the dtype's range before casting, or use a nullable type and a validation step.

topics.title: Series.to_numpy copies by default
topics.body: `to_numpy()` may share memory for a single dtype, and `copy=True` makes the boundary explicit. Knowing which you got matters when a model or a library writes into the array.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2])
arr = s.to_numpy(copy=True)
arr[0] = 99
print(s.tolist())

topics.title: from_records builds a frame from rows
topics.body: `pd.DataFrame.from_records` accepts tuples or dicts with an explicit column list, which is how a database cursor becomes a frame without a second parse.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame.from_records([(1, "a"), (2, "b")], columns=["id", "name"])
print(df["name"].tolist())

topics.title: A SQL WHERE is a mask
topics.body: Every SQL clause has a Pandas equivalent: SELECT is column selection, WHERE a Boolean mask, GROUP BY `groupby`, JOIN `merge`. Translating clause by clause is how a query becomes a frame.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"], "v": [10, 5]})
print(df[df["v"] > 5]["city"].tolist())

topics.title: One-hot before the split, fit on train
topics.body: Encoding a category is stateless and safe on the full table only when the category list is fixed. Any statistic — a mean, a fill value, a quantile — must be fitted on training rows and applied to both.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 10.0]})
train, test = df.iloc[:3], df.iloc[3:]
mean = train["x"].mean()
print(round(float((test["x"] - mean).iloc[0]), 2))

interview.q: Where exactly is the DataFrame/Numpy boundary in a model pipeline?
interview.answer: After all row-level work — filtering, joining, encoding, splitting — and before the estimator. `to_numpy(dtype=float)` at that point gives the model an unambiguous numeric matrix, while the frame keeps the labels for reporting.

interview.q: How do you explain data leakage to a non-specialist?
interview.answer: It is marking your own homework: the preparation step was allowed to look at the answers it will be tested on. The score looks excellent and then collapses in production, because the information it relied on will not be there.

topics.title: Write the question before the query
topics.body: A written question names the grain, the metric and the comparison. Without it, a table can be technically correct and still not answer what was asked.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"user": [1, 1, 2], "minutes": [10, 20, 30]})
print("per user:", df.groupby("user")["minutes"].sum().mean())
print("per attempt:", df["minutes"].mean())

topics.title: A cleaning log is part of the deliverable
topics.body: Recording what was dropped and why is what makes a number reviewable. A log line is a count, a rule and a reason.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 2], "v": [1, 2, 3]})
clean = raw.drop_duplicates("id", keep="last")
print(len(raw), len(clean))

topics.title: Reproducible means rerunnable
topics.body: A stored seed and a fixed input make the same output tomorrow. Anything without one is a screenshot, not an analysis.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": range(6)})
a = df.sample(3, random_state=11)["x"].tolist()
b = df.sample(3, random_state=11)["x"].tolist()
print(a == b)

topics.title: Present the table, then the chart
topics.body: A stakeholder needs the number they can quote and the picture that explains it. Shipping only one of the two forces them to recompute or to trust blindly.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "passed": [True, False, True]})
report = df.groupby("city")["passed"].agg(learners="size", rate="mean").round(2)
print(report.to_dict("index"))

interview.q: How do you present one finding in 30 seconds?
interview.answer: Question, method in one clause, the number with its denominator, and the decision it supports. Stop there; the notebook is the backup, not the pitch.

interview.q: What is the most common mistake in a junior Pandas project?
interview.answer: Trusting a row count — counting attempts as users, or a fan-out join that silently multiplied rows. Checking grain and counts before every aggregate catches most of it.
